diseases.name: Alzheimer's disease
diseases.classification: Neurodegenerative disease (most common cause of dementia)
diseases.overview: Alzheimer's disease is a progressive neurodegenerative disease in which accumulation of abnormal proteins and loss of synapses and neurons gradually impair memory, thinking and, eventually, the ability to carry out everyday activities.
diseases.pathophysiology: Two hallmark pathologies are extracellular plaques of amyloid-beta and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles of hyperphosphorylated tau. Tangle pathology typically begins in the entorhinal cortex and hippocampus and later spreads to association cortex, which parallels the early memory-predominant symptoms. Synapse loss, neuroinflammation and vascular factors contribute.
diseases.causes: Most cases are late-onset and arise from a combination of age, genetic and environmental factors. A small proportion of early-onset cases are caused by inherited mutations (APP, PSEN1, PSEN2).
riskFactors: Family history; APOE ε4 allele increases risk
Cardiovascular risk factors (hypertension, diabetes) — associated with higher risk
diseases.regionsSummary: Medial temporal lobe (entorhinal cortex, hippocampus) early; later temporal, parietal (including precuneus/posterior cingulate) and frontal association cortex. Primary motor, sensory and visual cortex are relatively spared until late.
symptoms: Difficulty remembering recent events and conversations
Changes in mood, personality or behaviour
diseases.progression: Usually gradual over years, from mild cognitive symptoms to moderate and severe dementia with dependence on others for daily care. Rate of progression varies widely between individuals.
diagnosis: Clinical history from the person and an informant
Blood tests to exclude other causes (e.g. thyroid, vitamin B12)
In selected cases: amyloid/tau PET, CSF or blood biomarkers
diseases.imaging: MRI may show medial temporal (hippocampal) atrophy and generalised atrophy; FDG-PET often shows reduced metabolism in temporoparietal and posterior cingulate cortex. Imaging supports but does not by itself establish the diagnosis.
treatments: Cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine for symptoms
Anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies for selected people with early disease and confirmed amyloid pathology, with monitoring for side effects such as ARIA
Treatment of coexisting conditions (hearing loss, depression, vascular risk factors)
diseases.rehabilitation: Cognitive stimulation, occupational therapy, safety planning, caregiver education and support, and advance care planning.
complications: Swallowing difficulty and aspiration pneumonia in late stages
diseases.prognosis: Progressive and currently not curable. Survival after diagnosis varies widely depending on age and other health conditions.
diseases.prevention: No intervention is proven to prevent Alzheimer's disease. Managing cardiovascular risk factors, physical activity, and social and cognitive engagement are associated with healthier brain ageing and are under active study.
diseases.emergingResearch: Blood-based biomarkers, anti-tau therapies and combination approaches are under investigation.

faq.q: Is memory loss always Alzheimer's disease?
faq.a: No. Memory problems have many causes, including other dementias, depression, medication effects, vitamin deficiency and normal ageing. A clinical evaluation is needed.

faq.q: Does the hippocampus shrink in everyone with Alzheimer's?
faq.a: Hippocampal atrophy is common but variable; atypical forms (e.g. posterior cortical or language-predominant variants) can begin elsewhere.

associations.explanation: Neurofibrillary tangles and neuronal loss affect the hippocampus early, matching early difficulty forming new memories.
Entorhinal cortex (anterior parahippocampal gyrus) is one of the earliest sites of tau pathology.
Pathology spreads to lateral temporal association cortex as disease advances.
Precuneus and parietal association cortex show reduced metabolism and atrophy; involvement is prominent in posterior variants.
Posterior cingulate hypometabolism is a frequent imaging feature.
Frontal association cortex is involved later, and earlier in some atypical presentations.

diseases.name: Parkinson's disease
diseases.overview: Parkinson's disease is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder best known for slowness of movement, rigidity, tremor at rest and postural instability, often accompanied by non-motor symptoms.
diseases.pathophysiology: Degeneration of dopamine-producing neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta reduces dopamine in the striatum (especially the putamen), disrupting basal ganglia–thalamocortical motor loops. Abnormal alpha-synuclein aggregates (Lewy bodies and neurites) are found in affected neurons and also in other brain regions and the peripheral autonomic nervous system.
diseases.causes: In most people the cause is unknown and likely involves genetic susceptibility with environmental factors. Several genes (for example LRRK2, GBA1, SNCA, PRKN) are associated with inherited or increased risk.
riskFactors: Family history and specific gene variants
Certain environmental exposures (e.g. some pesticides) — associations under study
diseases.regionsSummary: Substantia nigra pars compacta (within the midbrain cerebral peduncle region — not separately segmented in this model) and its striatal targets (putamen > caudate); Lewy pathology also affects brainstem nuclei and, later, limbic and cortical regions.
symptoms: Bradykinesia (slowness and reduced amplitude of movement)
Rest tremor, often starting on one side
Non-motor: reduced sense of smell, constipation, REM sleep behaviour disorder, depression, anxiety, cognitive changes
diseases.progression: Typically begins on one side and progresses slowly over years. Non-motor symptoms may precede motor diagnosis. Course and severity vary substantially.
diagnosis: Clinical diagnosis based on history and neurological examination
Response to dopaminergic medication supports the diagnosis
Imaging to exclude other causes when needed
Dopamine transporter imaging in selected uncertain cases
diseases.imaging: Routine MRI is often normal. Dopamine transporter SPECT can show reduced striatal uptake but does not distinguish Parkinson's disease from some other parkinsonian syndromes.
treatments: Dopamine agonists, MAO-B inhibitors, COMT inhibitors
Deep brain stimulation (subthalamic nucleus or globus pallidus internus) for selected patients
diseases.rehabilitation: Physiotherapy (gait, balance, exercise), occupational therapy, speech and swallowing therapy.
complications: Motor fluctuations and dyskinesia with long-term treatment
diseases.prognosis: Progressive but highly variable; many people maintain function for years with treatment.
diseases.prevention: No proven preventive measure. Regular physical activity is associated with lower risk and benefits people with the condition.
diseases.emergingResearch: Alpha-synuclein seed amplification assays, disease-modifying therapies targeting alpha-synuclein or LRRK2, and cell-based therapies are being studied.

faq.q: Why is the substantia nigra not highlighted on its own?
faq.a: The source anatomical model does not segment it separately; the cerebral peduncle element that contains it is highlighted as a schematic association.

associations.explanation: Contains the substantia nigra pars compacta, where dopaminergic neuron loss defines the disease. Schematic: the nigra itself is not segmented; the whole peduncle is NOT uniformly affected.
Loss of nigrostriatal dopamine is most marked in the putamen, producing the motor signs.
Dopamine depletion also affects the caudate, generally less than the putamen.
Altered pallidal output is part of basal ganglia circuit dysfunction; it is a DBS target.
Abnormal basal ganglia output alters thalamocortical motor signalling.
Lewy pathology often involves lower brainstem nuclei (e.g. dorsal motor nucleus of vagus), linked to non-motor symptoms.

diseases.name: Huntington's disease
diseases.overview: Huntington's disease is an inherited, progressive brain disorder that causes involuntary movements, psychiatric symptoms and cognitive decline.
diseases.pathophysiology: An expanded CAG trinucleotide repeat in the HTT gene produces mutant huntingtin protein. Medium spiny neurons of the striatum are particularly vulnerable, with early and marked degeneration of the caudate and putamen, followed by wider cortical involvement.
diseases.causes: Autosomal dominant inheritance: each child of an affected parent has a 50% chance of inheriting the expanded gene.
riskFactors: Having a parent with Huntington's disease
Longer CAG repeat length is associated with earlier onset
diseases.regionsSummary: Striatum (caudate nucleus earliest and most marked, then putamen); later cerebral cortex and other regions.
symptoms: Problems with planning, organisation and attention
diseases.progression: Typically begins in mid-adulthood and progresses over many years; a juvenile form begins before age 20.
diagnosis: Genetic testing for the HTT CAG expansion (with genetic counselling)
diseases.imaging: MRI/CT may show caudate atrophy with enlargement of the frontal horns of the lateral ventricles, and generalised atrophy later.
treatments: Medications to reduce chorea (e.g. VMAT2 inhibitors)
Treatment of depression, irritability and other psychiatric symptoms
No disease-modifying therapy is currently approved
diseases.rehabilitation: Physiotherapy, occupational and speech therapy, nutritional support, psychological and social support for families.
diseases.prognosis: Progressive; course typically spans many years after symptom onset.
diseases.prevention: No prevention of disease in gene carriers; genetic counselling and reproductive options are available for families.
diseases.emergingResearch: Huntingtin-lowering therapies (antisense oligonucleotides, gene therapies) are in clinical trials.

faq.q: Why does caudate shrinkage enlarge the ventricles?
faq.a: The caudate forms the lateral wall of the lateral ventricle; as it atrophies, the frontal horn expands.

associations.explanation: Earliest and most severe neuronal loss in the striatum, especially the caudate.
Putaminal medium spiny neurons also degenerate.
Downstream basal ganglia output is disrupted.
Frontal horns enlarge secondary to caudate atrophy (imaging sign, not primary pathology).
Cortical atrophy develops as disease advances, contributing to cognitive and behavioural symptoms.

diseases.name: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
diseases.overview: ALS is a progressive disease that destroys upper motor neurons in the brain and lower motor neurons in the brainstem and spinal cord, leading to weakness, muscle wasting and eventually respiratory failure.
diseases.pathophysiology: Degeneration of corticospinal (upper) motor neurons in the primary motor cortex and of lower motor neurons in brainstem motor nuclei and spinal anterior horns. TDP-43 protein aggregates are found in most cases. There is clinical and genetic overlap with frontotemporal dementia.
diseases.causes: Most cases are sporadic. About one in ten is familial; genes include C9orf72, SOD1, TARDBP and FUS.
riskFactors: Increasing age (peak onset in later middle age)
diseases.regionsSummary: Primary motor cortex (precentral gyrus) and corticospinal pathways (internal capsule, cerebral peduncles, pons, medulla), brainstem motor nuclei, spinal cord (not modelled); frontal and temporal cortex in ALS–FTD overlap.
symptoms: Slurred speech and swallowing difficulty (bulbar onset)
Cognitive or behavioural change in some people
diseases.progression: Progressive, with spread to other body regions. Rate varies considerably.
diagnosis: Clinical examination for upper and lower motor neuron signs
MRI and blood tests to exclude mimics
diseases.imaging: MRI is mainly used to exclude other causes; some people show signal change along the corticospinal tracts.
treatments: Riluzole and edaravone (disease-slowing therapies approved in some countries)
Non-invasive ventilation and nutritional support (e.g. gastrostomy)
diseases.rehabilitation: Multidisciplinary care: physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech and communication aids, respiratory care, palliative care.
diseases.prognosis: Progressive and life-limiting; survival varies widely, and a minority live many years.
diseases.prevention: No known prevention.
diseases.emergingResearch: Gene-targeted therapies (e.g. for C9orf72) and biomarkers such as neurofilament light are under study.

faq.q: Is ALS a disease of muscles?
faq.a: No. Muscles weaken because the motor neurons that control them degenerate.

associations.explanation: Upper motor neurons in primary motor cortex degenerate.
Descending corticospinal fibres degenerate along their course.
Corticospinal tract involvement (mainly posterior limb, which is not modelled; anterior limb shown for orientation only).
Brainstem motor nuclei (e.g. hypoglossal) are affected, causing bulbar symptoms.
Motor nuclei and descending tracts in the pons are involved.
Frontal involvement in people with ALS–FTD overlap.

diseases.name: Frontotemporal dementia
diseases.overview: Frontotemporal dementia is a group of disorders caused by progressive degeneration of the frontal and/or temporal lobes, producing changes in behaviour, personality or language.
diseases.pathophysiology: Neuronal loss with abnormal protein inclusions — most commonly tau, TDP-43 or (rarely) FUS — in frontal and anterior temporal cortex. The clinical variant depends on which regions degenerate first.
diseases.causes: Many cases are sporadic; a substantial proportion are familial, with mutations in genes such as MAPT, GRN and C9orf72.
riskFactors: Family history of FTD or ALS
Onset is often younger than in Alzheimer's disease
diseases.regionsSummary: Behavioural variant: frontal (especially orbitofrontal and medial) and anterior temporal cortex, insula. Semantic variant: anterior temporal lobe (often left). Non-fluent variant: left posterior frontal and insular cortex.
symptoms: Disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy (behavioural variant)
Relatively preserved memory early in many cases
diseases.progression: Progressive over years; symptoms broaden as degeneration spreads.
diseases.imaging: MRI may show focal frontal and/or anterior temporal atrophy, sometimes asymmetric; FDG-PET shows corresponding hypometabolism.
diseases.rehabilitation: Behavioural strategies, caregiver support and education, communication aids, safety planning.
complications: Coexisting motor neuron disease or parkinsonism in some people
diseases.prognosis: Progressive; duration varies by subtype and individual.
diseases.prevention: No known prevention.
diseases.emergingResearch: Gene-targeted therapies for GRN and C9orf72 mutation carriers are in trials.

faq.q: Is FTD the same as Alzheimer's disease?
faq.a: No. They differ in pathology, typical age of onset and early symptoms, although symptoms can overlap.

associations.explanation: Frontal atrophy underlies behavioural and executive changes.
Orbitofrontal cortex is commonly affected in the behavioural variant.
Anterior temporal atrophy is characteristic of the semantic variant.
Insular involvement is common, especially in behavioural and non-fluent variants.
Anterior cingulate involvement relates to apathy.

diseases.name: Dementia with Lewy bodies
synonyms: Lewy body dementia (umbrella term including Parkinson's disease dementia)
diseases.overview: Dementia with Lewy bodies is a progressive dementia characterised by fluctuating attention, visual hallucinations, REM sleep behaviour disorder and parkinsonism.
diseases.pathophysiology: Alpha-synuclein aggregates (Lewy bodies) accumulate in brainstem, limbic and neocortical neurons. Cholinergic deficits are prominent; coexisting Alzheimer-type pathology is common.
diseases.causes: Usually sporadic; genetic factors (e.g. GBA1, APOE ε4) increase risk.
diseases.regionsSummary: Distributed: brainstem (including substantia nigra), limbic structures (amygdala, cingulate) and neocortex; occipital hypometabolism is common on imaging. Hippocampus is often relatively preserved compared with Alzheimer's disease.
diseases.progression: Progressive; symptoms fluctuate day to day.
diagnosis: Clinical criteria based on core and supportive features
Dopamine transporter imaging, cardiac MIBG scintigraphy or polysomnography in selected cases
diseases.imaging: Relative preservation of medial temporal lobes on MRI compared with Alzheimer's disease; reduced striatal dopamine transporter uptake; occipital hypometabolism on FDG-PET.
treatments: Cautious use of levodopa for parkinsonism
Avoidance or extreme caution with antipsychotics
Treatment of sleep and autonomic symptoms
diseases.rehabilitation: Physiotherapy for falls prevention, occupational therapy, caregiver support.
diseases.prognosis: Progressive; course varies.
diseases.prevention: No known prevention.
diseases.emergingResearch: Alpha-synuclein biomarkers (skin biopsy, seed amplification assays) are being evaluated.

faq.q: How does DLB differ from Parkinson's disease dementia?
faq.a: By convention, DLB is diagnosed when dementia begins before or within about a year of parkinsonism; otherwise the term Parkinson's disease dementia is used.

associations.explanation: Substantia nigra (within this element; schematic) shows Lewy pathology and neuron loss, causing parkinsonism.
Limbic Lewy pathology is common.
Cingulate cortex is a typical site of cortical Lewy bodies.
Occipital hypometabolism on imaging, linked to visual symptoms; pathology is not uniform.
Reduced striatal dopamine transporter uptake reflects nigrostriatal degeneration.

diseases.name: Ischemic stroke
diseases.overview: An ischemic stroke occurs when blood flow to part of the brain is blocked, depriving brain tissue of oxygen and glucose. It is a medical emergency: rapid treatment can reduce brain damage.
diseases.pathophysiology: Arterial occlusion by thrombosis, embolism or small-vessel disease reduces perfusion. A core of irreversibly injured tissue may be surrounded by a penumbra of at-risk tissue that can be salvaged if flow is restored quickly. Deficits correspond to the vascular territory involved.
diseases.causes: Large-artery atherosclerosis, cardioembolism (e.g. atrial fibrillation), small-vessel (lacunar) disease, arterial dissection and other less common causes.
riskFactors: Atrial fibrillation and other heart disease
diseases.regionsSummary: Depends on the artery: middle cerebral artery territory (lateral frontal, parietal and temporal cortex, insula, deep basal ganglia and internal capsule) is most commonly affected; anterior cerebral (medial frontal/parietal), posterior cerebral (occipital, medial temporal, thalamus) and posterior circulation (brainstem, cerebellum) strokes also occur.
symptoms: Sudden weakness or numbness of face, arm or leg, especially on one side
Sudden dizziness, loss of balance or coordination
Sudden severe headache (more typical of haemorrhage)
diseases.progression: Onset is sudden. Deficits may improve over weeks to months with recovery and rehabilitation; some remain permanent.
diagnosis: Urgent brain imaging (CT or MRI) to exclude haemorrhage
CT or MR angiography to identify vessel occlusion
Cardiac evaluation and blood tests to find the cause
diseases.imaging: Early CT may be normal; diffusion-weighted MRI detects acute infarction within minutes to hours. Angiography shows occluded vessels.
treatments: Intravenous thrombolysis within established time windows for eligible patients
Mechanical thrombectomy for large-vessel occlusion in eligible patients
Antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy for secondary prevention as appropriate
Blood pressure, glucose and lipid management
diseases.rehabilitation: Physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech and language therapy and neuropsychological support, beginning early.
diseases.prognosis: Varies widely with stroke size, location, speed of treatment and rehabilitation.
diseases.prevention: Control of blood pressure, treatment of atrial fibrillation, not smoking, diabetes and cholesterol management, physical activity.
diseases.emergingResearch: Extended treatment windows guided by perfusion imaging and neuroprotective strategies are under study.

faq.q: What should I do if I suspect a stroke?
faq.a: Call emergency services immediately. This application cannot assess or diagnose a stroke.

associations.explanation: Lateral frontal cortex lies in the MCA territory; medial frontal in the ACA territory.
Lateral parietal cortex is commonly involved in MCA strokes.
Lateral temporal cortex lies in the MCA territory.
Insula is frequently involved in proximal MCA occlusion.
Deep lenticulostriate branches supply the basal nuclei; lacunar infarcts are common here.
Small capsular infarcts can cause marked weakness.
Posterior cerebral artery strokes cause contralateral visual field loss.
Thalamic infarcts arise from posterior circulation branches.
Vertebrobasilar strokes affect the brainstem.
Cerebellar infarcts cause ataxia and can cause dangerous swelling.

diseases.name: Hemorrhagic stroke
diseases.overview: A hemorrhagic stroke occurs when a blood vessel ruptures and bleeds into or around the brain. Intracerebral haemorrhage bleeds into brain tissue; subarachnoid haemorrhage (covered separately) bleeds around it.
diseases.pathophysiology: Blood forms a haematoma that destroys and compresses surrounding tissue, raises intracranial pressure and can expand in the first hours. Chronic hypertension damages small penetrating arteries, explaining the typical deep locations.
diseases.causes: Chronic hypertension (deep haemorrhages), cerebral amyloid angiopathy (lobar haemorrhages in older adults), anticoagulant use, vascular malformations, tumours, and drug use (e.g. cocaine).
diseases.regionsSummary: Hypertensive haemorrhages: putamen, thalamus, pons and cerebellum. Amyloid angiopathy: cortical-subcortical (lobar) regions.
diseases.progression: Sudden onset; early deterioration can occur from haematoma expansion or swelling.
diagnosis: CT/MR angiography to look for an underlying vascular lesion
diseases.imaging: CT shows acute blood as a hyperdense area; MRI sequences can detect old microbleeds suggesting the underlying cause.
treatments: Blood pressure lowering according to guidelines
Neurosurgery in selected cases (e.g. cerebellar haemorrhage)
diseases.rehabilitation: Multidisciplinary stroke rehabilitation.
diseases.prognosis: Depends on haematoma size, location, consciousness level and age; often more severe than ischaemic stroke.
diseases.prevention: Blood pressure control is the most important preventive measure.
diseases.emergingResearch: Minimally invasive haematoma evacuation and haemostatic therapies are being studied.

faq.q: Can a stroke be identified as haemorrhagic without a scan?
faq.a: No. Brain imaging is required to distinguish haemorrhagic from ischaemic stroke.

associations.explanation: Most common site of hypertensive haemorrhage.
Common site of hypertensive haemorrhage.
Pontine haemorrhage can be devastating.
Cerebellar haemorrhage may require urgent surgery.
Lobar (subcortical) haemorrhages occur with amyloid angiopathy.
Blood may extend into the ventricles and cause hydrocephalus.

diseases.reviewStatus: Draft — educational summary from cited sources; pending clinical reviewer sign-off.

diseases.name: Subarachnoid hemorrhage
diseases.overview: Subarachnoid haemorrhage is bleeding into the subarachnoid space between the arachnoid membrane and the brain surface, most often from a ruptured aneurysm when not caused by trauma.
diseases.pathophysiology: Blood under arterial pressure enters CSF spaces around the base of the brain, causing a sudden rise in intracranial pressure, meningeal irritation and possible later complications such as vasospasm and hydrocephalus.
diseases.causes: Ruptured cerebral aneurysm (most common non-traumatic cause), head injury, arteriovenous malformation, and other less common causes.
riskFactors: Polycystic kidney disease and some connective tissue disorders
diseases.regionsSummary: Subarachnoid spaces around the brain (not modelled as structures). Secondary effects may involve the ventricular system (hydrocephalus) and any territory affected by delayed ischaemia.
diseases.progression: Abrupt onset; risk of rebleeding and delayed complications in the following days to weeks.
diagnosis: Lumbar puncture if CT is negative but suspicion remains
CT angiography or catheter angiography to find the source
diseases.imaging: CT shows blood in the basal cisterns and sulci; angiography identifies aneurysms.
treatments: Securing a ruptured aneurysm by endovascular coiling or surgical clipping
Nimodipine to reduce delayed ischaemic complications
diseases.rehabilitation: Rehabilitation for physical and cognitive deficits; support for fatigue and mood.
diseases.prognosis: Variable; depends on severity at presentation, age and complications.
diseases.prevention: Blood pressure control and not smoking; management of known aneurysms by specialists.
diseases.emergingResearch: Strategies to prevent delayed cerebral ischaemia are under investigation.

faq.q: Why isn't a structure highlighted for the bleed itself?
faq.a: The bleed is in the subarachnoid space around the brain, which is not a segmented structure in the model. The ventricles are shown as a secondary association (hydrocephalus).

associations.explanation: Hydrocephalus after SAH enlarges the ventricular system.
Ventricular enlargement from impaired CSF absorption or flow.
Delayed ischaemia or haematoma can affect territories near the ruptured aneurysm, e.g. anterior communicating artery aneurysms near the medial frontal lobes.

diseases.reviewStatus: Draft — educational summary from cited sources; pending clinical reviewer sign-off.

diseases.name: Cerebral aneurysm
diseases.overview: A cerebral aneurysm is a weak, bulging area in the wall of an artery in the brain. Most never rupture, but rupture causes subarachnoid haemorrhage.
diseases.pathophysiology: Saccular aneurysms usually form at branch points of arteries in the circle of Willis, where haemodynamic stress and wall weakness combine. Size, location, shape and growth influence rupture risk.
diseases.causes: Acquired wall degeneration; associated with genetic and connective tissue conditions in some people.
diseases.regionsSummary: Arteries of the circle of Willis at the base of the brain (vessels are not modelled). Large aneurysms can compress nearby structures such as the optic chiasm or nerves.
symptoms: Large unruptured aneurysms: headache, vision changes, eye movement problems from nerve compression
Rupture: sudden severe headache (see subarachnoid haemorrhage)
diseases.progression: Many remain stable; some grow. Rupture is a sudden event.
diseases.imaging: Angiographic imaging shows the aneurysm sac and its relation to parent vessels.
treatments: Observation with imaging surveillance for selected small aneurysms
diseases.rehabilitation: Only needed after rupture or treatment complications.
diseases.prognosis: Unruptured aneurysms often have a good outlook; ruptured aneurysms carry serious risk.
diseases.prevention: Not smoking and blood pressure control reduce growth and rupture risk.
diseases.emergingResearch: Better tools for predicting rupture risk are being developed.

faq.q: Does everyone with an aneurysm need surgery?
faq.a: No. Specialists weigh size, location, shape and personal factors.

associations.explanation: Large aneurysms near the circle of Willis can compress the chiasm, causing visual field loss.
Posterior communicating artery aneurysms can compress the oculomotor nerve as it leaves the midbrain (nerve not modelled).

diseases.reviewStatus: Draft — educational summary from cited sources; pending clinical reviewer sign-off.

diseases.name: Cerebral arteriovenous malformation
diseases.overview: A brain AVM is a tangle of abnormal blood vessels in which arteries connect directly to veins without an intervening capillary bed.
diseases.pathophysiology: High-flow shunting through a nidus of abnormal vessels can lead to haemorrhage, seizures through irritation of surrounding cortex, or deficits from altered blood flow.
diseases.causes: Usually thought to arise during development; most are not inherited. Some occur in hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia.
diseases.regionsSummary: Can occur anywhere in the brain; cerebral hemispheres are most common. Location strongly influences symptoms and treatment options.
diseases.progression: May remain silent for years; haemorrhage risk persists over a lifetime.
diagnosis: Catheter angiography to define the architecture
diseases.imaging: Flow voids on MRI and a vascular nidus with early draining veins on angiography.
diseases.rehabilitation: After haemorrhage or treatment as needed.
diseases.prognosis: Varies with size, location, venous drainage and haemorrhage history.
diseases.prevention: No known prevention.
diseases.emergingResearch: Molecular studies of AVM formation (e.g. KRAS mutations) may lead to drug therapies.

faq.q: Where is the AVM in the model?
faq.a: AVMs are patient-specific and vessels are not modelled, so no structure is highlighted as affected.

associations.explanation: Most brain AVMs are located in the cerebral hemispheres; exact site varies by patient.

diseases.name: Epilepsy
diseases.classification: Chronic neurological disease (tendency to recurrent unprovoked seizures)
diseases.overview: Epilepsy is a brain condition characterised by an enduring predisposition to recurrent unprovoked seizures. A seizure is a transient episode of abnormal, excessive or synchronous neuronal activity.
diseases.pathophysiology: An imbalance between excitation and inhibition in neural networks allows abnormal synchronous discharges. Seizures may start in one network (focal) or engage bilateral networks from onset (generalised).
diseases.causes: Structural (stroke, tumour, trauma, malformations, hippocampal sclerosis), genetic, infectious, metabolic, immune, or unknown.
diseases.regionsSummary: Any cortical network can be involved. Focal epilepsies most often arise from the temporal and frontal lobes; generalised epilepsies involve bilateral thalamocortical networks.
symptoms: Seizures that vary by type: convulsions, staring spells, brief jerks, altered awareness, unusual sensations or emotions
diseases.progression: Many people become seizure-free with treatment; some epilepsies are drug-resistant.
diagnosis: Blood tests and genetic testing as indicated
diseases.imaging: MRI may reveal a cause (e.g. hippocampal sclerosis, cortical dysplasia, tumour) but is normal in many people.
treatments: Epilepsy surgery for selected drug-resistant focal epilepsy
Neuromodulation (vagus nerve, responsive or deep brain stimulation)
diseases.rehabilitation: Education, safety planning, psychological support, attention to memory and mood.
diseases.prognosis: Highly variable by cause and syndrome.
diseases.prevention: Preventing head injury, stroke and CNS infections reduces some acquired epilepsies.
diseases.emergingResearch: Gene therapies for specific genetic epilepsies and closed-loop stimulation.

faq.q: Is one seizure the same as epilepsy?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Epilepsy implies an enduring tendency to recurrent unprovoked seizures; a clinician makes this diagnosis.

associations.explanation: The most common origin of focal seizures in adults.
Second most common origin of focal seizures.
Thalamocortical networks are central to generalised seizures such as absence seizures.
Hippocampal sclerosis is a common cause of drug-resistant temporal lobe epilepsy.

diseases.reviewStatus: Draft — educational summary from cited sources; pending clinical reviewer sign-off.

diseases.name: Temporal lobe epilepsy
diseases.overview: Temporal lobe epilepsy is a form of focal epilepsy in which seizures arise from the temporal lobe — most often its medial structures.
diseases.pathophysiology: Medial temporal lobe epilepsy is frequently associated with hippocampal sclerosis (neuronal loss and gliosis). Lateral (neocortical) TLE arises from lateral temporal cortex.
diseases.causes: Hippocampal sclerosis, tumours, vascular malformations, cortical dysplasia, prior infection or injury, autoimmune encephalitis, or unknown.
riskFactors: History of prolonged febrile seizures in childhood (association with hippocampal sclerosis)
diseases.regionsSummary: Hippocampus, amygdala and parahippocampal gyrus (medial TLE); lateral temporal neocortex (lateral TLE).
symptoms: Auras such as a rising abdominal sensation, déjà vu, fear, or unusual smells
Post-ictal confusion; language difficulty if dominant side
diseases.progression: May respond to medication; medial TLE with hippocampal sclerosis is often drug-resistant.
diagnosis: Neuropsychological testing and functional imaging before surgery
diseases.imaging: Hippocampal sclerosis appears as hippocampal atrophy with increased T2/FLAIR signal on MRI.
treatments: Anterior temporal lobectomy or selective amygdalohippocampectomy for drug-resistant cases
diseases.rehabilitation: Memory strategies, psychological support.
diseases.prognosis: Surgery offers a good chance of seizure freedom for well-selected patients; outcomes vary.
diseases.prevention: Not generally preventable.
diseases.emergingResearch: Minimally invasive ablation techniques and network mapping.

faq.q: Does every person with TLE have hippocampal sclerosis?
faq.a: No. It is common in medial TLE, but other causes exist and some people have normal MRI.

associations.explanation: Hippocampal sclerosis is the most common pathology in medial TLE.
Seizures often involve the amygdala, producing emotional auras.
Part of the medial temporal seizure network.
Lateral temporal neocortex in lateral TLE.

diseases.reviewStatus: Draft — educational summary from cited sources; pending clinical reviewer sign-off.

diseases.name: Focal epilepsy
diseases.classification: Epilepsy type (seizures originating in one hemisphere's network)
diseases.overview: In focal epilepsy, seizures start within networks limited to one hemisphere. Symptoms reflect the function of the region where seizures begin and spread.
diseases.pathophysiology: A localised epileptogenic zone generates abnormal discharges that may remain focal or spread to bilateral networks (focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizure).
diseases.causes: Structural lesions (tumour, stroke, trauma, dysplasia, hippocampal sclerosis), infections, immune causes, genetic causes, or unknown.
riskFactors: Prior brain injury, stroke or infection
diseases.regionsSummary: Any cortical region; temporal and frontal lobes are most common. The motor features depend on location (e.g. precentral gyrus seizures cause contralateral jerking).
symptoms: Focal aware seizures (e.g. jerking, tingling, visual phenomena)
diseases.progression: Variable; depends on cause.
diseases.imaging: MRI may show the causative lesion.
treatments: Resective or ablative surgery for drug-resistant cases with an identified focus
diseases.rehabilitation: Depends on deficits and comorbidities.
diseases.prognosis: Variable.
diseases.prevention: Prevention of underlying causes where possible.
diseases.emergingResearch: Improved localisation with high-density EEG and stereo-EEG.

faq.q: Why does a seizure in one area cause specific symptoms?
faq.a: Because the seizure temporarily disrupts or activates the functions of that region — for example, visual phenomena from occipital cortex.

associations.explanation: Most common lobe of seizure onset.
Frontal lobe seizures are often brief and may occur in sleep.
Parietal seizures can cause sensory symptoms.
Occipital seizures can cause visual phenomena.

diseases.reviewStatus: Draft — educational summary from cited sources; pending clinical reviewer sign-off.

diseases.name: Generalized epilepsy
diseases.classification: Epilepsy type (seizures engaging bilateral networks from onset)
diseases.overview: In generalised epilepsy, seizures arise within and rapidly engage bilaterally distributed networks, including thalamocortical circuits.
diseases.pathophysiology: Abnormal oscillations in thalamocortical networks underlie seizure types such as absence seizures (spike-and-wave discharges); many generalised epilepsies have a genetic basis.
diseases.causes: Often genetic (polygenic or single-gene); sometimes metabolic or structural.
diseases.regionsSummary: Bilateral, distributed networks: thalamus and widespread cortex — not a single focal region.
symptoms: Atonic or tonic seizures in some syndromes
diseases.progression: Some childhood syndromes remit; others persist into adulthood.
diagnosis: MRI usually normal in genetic generalised epilepsies
diseases.imaging: Usually normal in genetic generalised epilepsies.
treatments: Avoidance of triggers such as sleep deprivation
diseases.rehabilitation: Education and safety measures.
diseases.prognosis: Often good with appropriate medication; varies by syndrome.
diseases.prevention: Trigger management.
diseases.emergingResearch: Precision therapies for specific genetic causes.

faq.q: Why is the whole cortex not shown as 'damaged'?
faq.a: Generalised epilepsy reflects abnormal network activity, usually without structural damage; the highlight indicates network involvement only.

associations.explanation: Thalamocortical circuits generate generalised spike-and-wave discharges.
Bilateral cortical networks are engaged from seizure onset; this is functional, not structural, involvement.

diseases.reviewStatus: Draft — educational summary from cited sources; pending clinical reviewer sign-off.

diseases.name: Multiple sclerosis
diseases.classification: Chronic immune-mediated demyelinating disease of the CNS
diseases.overview: Multiple sclerosis is a chronic disease in which the immune system damages myelin and axons in the brain, optic nerves and spinal cord, causing episodes or progression of neurological symptoms.
diseases.pathophysiology: Immune cells enter the CNS and cause focal inflammatory demyelinating lesions (plaques) with variable axonal loss. Lesions are microscopic to centimetre-sized and scattered in time and space; they do not affect whole anatomical structures. Progressive forms involve diffuse neurodegeneration.
diseases.causes: Unknown; combination of genetic susceptibility and environmental factors.
diseases.regionsSummary: Scattered white-matter lesions, typically periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial (brainstem, cerebellum) and in the optic nerves and spinal cord; the corpus callosum is often involved. Cortical lesions also occur.
symptoms: Vision loss with painful eye movement (optic neuritis)
diseases.progression: Most commonly relapsing-remitting at onset; some people later develop secondary progression; a minority have primary progressive MS.
diagnosis: MRI demonstrating dissemination in space and time (established criteria)
diseases.imaging: Ovoid T2/FLAIR lesions perpendicular to the ventricles, juxtacortical and infratentorial lesions; gadolinium-enhancing lesions indicate active inflammation.
treatments: Disease-modifying therapies (injectable, oral and infusion) to reduce relapses and new lesions
diseases.rehabilitation: Physiotherapy, occupational therapy, cognitive rehabilitation, fatigue management.
diseases.prognosis: Highly variable; disease-modifying therapies have changed long-term outlook.
diseases.prevention: No proven prevention; not smoking is advised.
diseases.emergingResearch: Remyelination therapies, BTK inhibitors, and EBV-targeted approaches are under investigation.

faq.q: Can demyelination be seen on the 3D model?
faq.a: No. Demyelination is microscopic; the model highlights typical lesion locations schematically, and the separate axon animation explains the process.

associations.explanation: Focal lesions are scattered through hemispheric white matter, especially periventricular and juxtacortical regions — not the entire white matter.
Callosal lesions are characteristic.
Optic neuritis is a common presentation.
Marks the periventricular location of typical lesions (the ventricle itself is not diseased).
Infratentorial lesions cause double vision, vertigo and other brainstem symptoms.
Cerebellar and peduncular lesions cause ataxia and tremor.

diseases.name: Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis
diseases.overview: ADEM is a brief but intense attack of inflammation in the brain and spinal cord that damages myelin, typically following an infection and most common in children.
diseases.pathophysiology: An immune response — often after infection — targets CNS myelin, producing widespread, often large and poorly marginated white matter and deep grey matter lesions. Antibodies to MOG are found in a subset.
diseases.causes: Often follows viral or bacterial infection; rarely after vaccination; frequently no trigger is identified.
diseases.regionsSummary: Multifocal white matter of the cerebral hemispheres, deep grey matter (thalamus, basal ganglia), brainstem, cerebellum and spinal cord.
diseases.progression: Usually monophasic; some people have recurrences or are later diagnosed with MS or MOG antibody-associated disease.
diagnosis: Testing for MOG and aquaporin-4 antibodies
Exclusion of infection and other causes
diseases.imaging: Large, bilateral, asymmetric T2/FLAIR lesions in white and deep grey matter, typically of similar age.
treatments: Intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange if steroids fail
diseases.rehabilitation: Physical, occupational and cognitive rehabilitation as needed.
diseases.prognosis: Many people, especially children, recover substantially; outcomes vary.
diseases.prevention: No specific prevention.
diseases.emergingResearch: Defining MOG antibody-associated disease as a distinct entity.

faq.q: How is ADEM different from MS?
faq.a: ADEM is usually a single episode with encephalopathy and widespread lesions of similar age; MS involves recurrent attacks over time.

associations.explanation: Multifocal white matter lesions — not the whole white matter.
Deep grey matter lesions are common.
Basal ganglia may be involved.
Brainstem lesions occur.
Cerebellar involvement causes ataxia.

diseases.name: Autoimmune encephalitis
diseases.classification: Group of immune-mediated inflammatory brain disorders
diseases.overview: Autoimmune encephalitis is a group of conditions in which the immune system attacks brain cells, causing inflammation and symptoms such as memory loss, behaviour change and seizures.
diseases.pathophysiology: Antibodies target neuronal surface proteins (e.g. NMDA receptor, LGI1) or intracellular antigens (often paraneoplastic, T-cell mediated). Limbic structures are frequently affected.
diseases.causes: Can be triggered by tumours (paraneoplastic), infections (e.g. after herpes simplex encephalitis) or occur without a known trigger.
riskFactors: Certain tumours (e.g. ovarian teratoma for anti-NMDAR)
Personal or family history of autoimmunity
diseases.regionsSummary: Limbic encephalitis: medial temporal lobes (hippocampus, amygdala). Anti-NMDAR encephalitis often has normal or non-specific MRI despite widespread network dysfunction.
diseases.progression: Develops over days to weeks; may relapse.
diagnosis: Neural antibody testing in serum and CSF
diseases.imaging: May show T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the medial temporal lobes; frequently normal in some subtypes.
treatments: Immunotherapy (corticosteroids, IVIG, plasma exchange; second-line agents)
diseases.rehabilitation: Cognitive, psychological and physical rehabilitation; recovery can take months.
diseases.prognosis: Many people recover with treatment; outcome varies by subtype and time to treatment.
diseases.prevention: None specific.
diseases.emergingResearch: Discovery of new antibodies and targeted immunotherapies.

faq.q: Is autoimmune encephalitis an infection?
faq.a: No. It is caused by the immune system, although infection can sometimes trigger it.

associations.explanation: Limbic encephalitis commonly involves the hippocampi, causing memory loss and seizures.
Amygdala inflammation is common in limbic encephalitis.
Medial temporal involvement; extent varies by antibody.

diseases.reviewStatus: Draft — educational summary from cited sources; pending clinical reviewer sign-off.

diseases.name: Meningitis
diseases.classification: Infection/inflammation of the meninges (medical emergency when bacterial)
diseases.overview: Meningitis is inflammation of the membranes (meninges) covering the brain and spinal cord, usually due to infection. Bacterial meningitis is a medical emergency.
diseases.pathophysiology: Pathogens reach the subarachnoid space, triggering inflammation in the meninges and CSF. Complications arise from raised intracranial pressure, vasculitis, and impaired CSF absorption.
diseases.causes: Viruses (most common, often milder), bacteria (e.g. Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis), fungi, and non-infectious causes.
diseases.regionsSummary: Meninges and subarachnoid space surrounding the whole brain (not modelled). Secondary effects can include hydrocephalus and cortical or cranial nerve involvement.
symptoms: In infants: irritability, poor feeding, bulging fontanelle
diseases.progression: Bacterial meningitis can progress within hours; viral meningitis is usually self-limiting.
diagnosis: Brain imaging before lumbar puncture in selected patients
diseases.imaging: Often normal; may show meningeal enhancement or complications.
treatments: Immediate intravenous antibiotics for suspected bacterial meningitis
diseases.rehabilitation: Hearing assessment and rehabilitation; cognitive and physical therapy after severe illness.
diseases.prognosis: Varies greatly with cause and speed of treatment.
diseases.prevention: Vaccination (e.g. pneumococcal, meningococcal, Hib); prophylactic antibiotics for close contacts of some bacterial cases.
diseases.emergingResearch: Rapid molecular diagnostics.

faq.q: Why are no brain structures highlighted as primary?
faq.a: Meningitis affects the membranes around the brain, which are not modelled; secondary effects are shown.

associations.explanation: Hydrocephalus can complicate meningitis.
The meninges overlying the hemispheres are inflamed; cortex beneath can be secondarily affected.

diseases.reviewStatus: Draft — educational summary from cited sources; pending clinical reviewer sign-off.

diseases.name: Encephalitis
diseases.classification: Inflammation of brain tissue (infectious or immune)
diseases.overview: Encephalitis is inflammation of the brain itself, most often caused by viral infection or an autoimmune process. This entry focuses on infectious encephalitis.
diseases.pathophysiology: Viruses infect brain tissue directly, causing inflammation, neuronal injury and swelling. Herpes simplex virus has a predilection for the medial temporal and inferior frontal lobes and insula.
diseases.causes: Herpes simplex virus, varicella zoster, enteroviruses, arthropod-borne viruses (e.g. West Nile), and others; autoimmune causes are covered separately.
riskFactors: Mosquito or tick exposure in endemic areas
Lack of vaccination for preventable causes
diseases.regionsSummary: Herpes simplex encephalitis: medial temporal lobes, orbitofrontal cortex, insula (often asymmetric). Other viruses show different patterns (e.g. thalamus, basal ganglia, brainstem).
diseases.progression: Develops over hours to days; may be life-threatening.
diagnosis: Lumbar puncture with PCR for viruses
diseases.imaging: HSV encephalitis typically shows T2/FLAIR signal change in the medial temporal lobes and insula.
treatments: Empirical intravenous aciclovir when HSV is suspected
diseases.rehabilitation: Cognitive, memory and physical rehabilitation.
diseases.prognosis: Depends on the cause and speed of treatment.
diseases.prevention: Vaccination for preventable causes; avoiding mosquito and tick bites.
diseases.emergingResearch: Metagenomic sequencing to identify causative organisms.

faq.q: Why are temporal structures highlighted?
faq.a: They are typical targets of herpes simplex encephalitis, the most common identified sporadic cause in many countries. Other viruses affect other regions.

associations.explanation: HSV encephalitis commonly affects medial temporal structures.
Involved in HSV encephalitis.
Insula is characteristically involved in HSV encephalitis.
Inferior frontal involvement in HSV encephalitis.
Some arboviral encephalitides involve the thalamus and basal ganglia.

diseases.name: Brain abscess
diseases.overview: A brain abscess is a collection of pus and infected material within the brain, usually caused by bacteria or fungi.
diseases.pathophysiology: Organisms reach the brain by spread from nearby infection (sinuses, ears, teeth), through the bloodstream, or after trauma or surgery. Focal cerebritis evolves into a capsule-enclosed abscess that acts as a mass lesion.
diseases.causes: Bacteria (streptococci, anaerobes, staphylococci), fungi and parasites, especially in immunocompromised people.
riskFactors: Congenital heart disease with right-to-left shunt
diseases.regionsSummary: Location depends on source: frontal lobe (sinus/dental), temporal lobe and cerebellum (ear infections); haematogenous abscesses are often at the grey–white junction and may be multiple.
diseases.progression: Develops over days to weeks; rupture into the ventricles is dangerous.
diagnosis: MRI with contrast (diffusion-weighted imaging helps distinguish abscess from tumour)
diseases.imaging: Ring-enhancing lesion with surrounding oedema and restricted diffusion in the centre.
diseases.rehabilitation: As needed for deficits.
diseases.prognosis: Improved with modern imaging and treatment; depends on size, location and patient factors.
diseases.prevention: Prompt treatment of sinus, ear and dental infections.
diseases.emergingResearch: Molecular pathogen identification.

faq.q: Is the highlighted lobe entirely infected?
faq.a: No. An abscess is a focal lesion; the highlight indicates typical locations only.

associations.explanation: Common site from frontal sinus or dental spread.
Common site from middle ear or mastoid infection.
Can arise from ear infections.

diseases.reviewStatus: Draft — educational summary from cited sources; pending clinical reviewer sign-off.

diseases.name: Glioblastoma
diseases.classification: Malignant primary brain tumour (CNS WHO grade 4 glioma)
diseases.overview: Glioblastoma is the most common malignant primary brain tumour in adults. It grows rapidly and infiltrates surrounding brain tissue.
diseases.pathophysiology: Arises from glial lineage cells. Defined in current classification as an IDH-wildtype diffuse astrocytic glioma with specific histological or molecular features. Tumour cells infiltrate along white matter tracts, including across the corpus callosum ('butterfly' pattern).
diseases.causes: Mostly unknown. Prior high-dose ionising radiation to the head and rare inherited syndromes increase risk.
diseases.regionsSummary: Usually supratentorial cerebral hemispheres (frontal and temporal lobes most often), infiltrating white matter; may cross the corpus callosum.
symptoms: Focal deficits such as weakness or speech difficulty
diseases.progression: Rapid growth over weeks to months; recurrence after treatment is common.
diagnosis: Biopsy or surgical resection with histological and molecular analysis
diseases.imaging: Heterogeneous ring-enhancing mass with central necrosis and surrounding oedema/infiltration.
treatments: Radiotherapy with concurrent and adjuvant temozolomide chemotherapy
diseases.rehabilitation: Physical, occupational and speech therapy; palliative and supportive care.
diseases.prognosis: Generally poor despite treatment; varies with age, performance status, extent of resection and molecular features (e.g. MGMT promoter methylation).
diseases.prevention: No known prevention.
diseases.emergingResearch: Immunotherapies, targeted therapies and vaccines are under investigation.

faq.q: Does the highlighted lobe mean the whole lobe is tumour?
faq.a: No. Tumour location varies by patient; the model shows common sites schematically.

associations.explanation: One of the most common locations.
One of the most common locations.
Infiltrates along white matter tracts.
Can spread across the corpus callosum to the other hemisphere.

diseases.reviewStatus: Draft — educational summary from cited sources; pending clinical reviewer sign-off.

diseases.name: Meningioma
diseases.classification: Primary tumour of the meninges (most often benign, CNS WHO grade 1)
diseases.overview: A meningioma is a tumour arising from the meninges, the membranes surrounding the brain and spinal cord. Most grow slowly and are benign, but they can cause symptoms by compressing adjacent brain or nerves.
diseases.pathophysiology: Arises from arachnoid cap cells. Effects are mainly due to compression of adjacent structures (mass effect) rather than invasion of brain tissue.
diseases.causes: Mostly unknown; prior cranial radiation and neurofibromatosis type 2 increase risk; hormonal factors may play a role.
diseases.regionsSummary: Outside the brain along dural surfaces: convexity, parasagittal/falx, sphenoid wing, olfactory groove, skull base. Symptoms reflect the compressed region (e.g. frontal lobe, optic apparatus).
diseases.progression: Usually slow; higher-grade meningiomas grow faster and recur more often.
diseases.imaging: Extra-axial, well-circumscribed, homogeneously enhancing mass often with a dural tail.
diseases.rehabilitation: As needed after surgery.
complications: Neurological deficits from compression or surgery
diseases.prognosis: Generally favourable for grade 1 tumours; depends on grade and resectability.
diseases.prevention: No known prevention.
diseases.emergingResearch: Molecular classification to better predict recurrence.

faq.q: Is a meningioma a brain tumour?
faq.a: It is classified among brain tumours but arises from the coverings of the brain, not brain tissue itself.

associations.explanation: Convexity, parasagittal and olfactory groove meningiomas can compress the frontal lobe.
Skull-base (e.g. tuberculum sellae) meningiomas can compress the optic apparatus.
Parasagittal and convexity tumours can compress parietal cortex.

diseases.name: Astrocytoma
diseases.overview: Astrocytomas are tumours arising from astrocyte-lineage glial cells. They range from slow-growing circumscribed tumours (such as pilocytic astrocytoma, common in children) to diffusely infiltrating tumours graded 2–4.
diseases.pathophysiology: Adult diffuse astrocytomas are defined by IDH mutation and graded by histological and molecular features. Pilocytic astrocytomas are typically circumscribed and associated with MAPK pathway alterations.
diseases.causes: Mostly unknown; neurofibromatosis type 1 increases risk of some types.
diseases.regionsSummary: Adult diffuse astrocytomas: cerebral hemispheres. Pilocytic astrocytomas: cerebellum, optic pathway, hypothalamus and brainstem, especially in children.
diseases.progression: Ranges from very slow to rapid depending on type and grade.
diseases.imaging: Varies by type: diffuse astrocytomas often non-enhancing T2/FLAIR-bright infiltrative lesions; pilocytic astrocytomas often cyst with an enhancing nodule.
treatments: Radiotherapy and chemotherapy depending on grade
Targeted therapies for specific molecular alterations (e.g. IDH inhibitors in selected cases)
diseases.rehabilitation: As needed.
diseases.prognosis: Varies widely by type, grade and molecular features.
diseases.prevention: No known prevention.
diseases.emergingResearch: IDH-targeted therapies.

faq.q: Why are children's and adults' astrocytomas shown in different places?
faq.a: Different tumour types predominate in different age groups and locations.

associations.explanation: Adult diffuse astrocytomas typically arise in the cerebral hemispheres.
Pilocytic astrocytoma commonly arises in the cerebellum in children.
Optic pathway gliomas (often pilocytic) occur, particularly with NF1.
Brainstem gliomas occur, especially in children.

diseases.name: Brain metastases
diseases.overview: Brain metastases are tumours that spread to the brain from cancer elsewhere in the body. They are more common than primary brain tumours in adults.
diseases.pathophysiology: Cancer cells reach the brain through the bloodstream and tend to lodge at the grey–white matter junction and in arterial border zones; distribution roughly follows blood flow, so most are supratentorial.
diseases.causes: Common primary cancers include lung, breast, melanoma, kidney and colorectal cancer.
riskFactors: Specific primary tumour types and molecular subtypes
diseases.regionsSummary: Grey–white matter junction of the cerebral hemispheres (most), cerebellum (minority); often multiple.
diseases.progression: Depends on the primary cancer and treatment response.
diseases.imaging: One or more well-circumscribed enhancing lesions at the grey–white junction with surrounding oedema.
treatments: Systemic targeted or immunotherapies with CNS activity
diseases.rehabilitation: Supportive and rehabilitative care.
diseases.prognosis: Varies widely with primary cancer type, number of lesions and systemic disease control.
diseases.prevention: Screening MRI in high-risk cancers allows earlier treatment.
diseases.emergingResearch: CNS-penetrant targeted therapies.

faq.q: Is metastatic brain cancer the same as the original cancer?
faq.a: Yes — the tumour cells are from the primary cancer, which guides treatment.

associations.explanation: Most metastases occur in the cerebral hemispheres, often at the grey–white junction.
A minority occur in the cerebellum.

diseases.name: Traumatic brain injury
diseases.classification: Acquired brain injury (spectrum from mild to severe)
diseases.overview: Traumatic brain injury is a disruption of normal brain function caused by an external force such as a blow, jolt or penetrating injury to the head.
diseases.pathophysiology: Primary injury (contusion, haemorrhage, axonal shearing) occurs at impact; secondary injury evolves over hours to days through swelling, ischaemia, excitotoxicity and inflammation. Contusions are typical where the brain meets bony ridges.
diseases.causes: Falls, road traffic collisions, assaults, sports, blast injuries.
diseases.regionsSummary: Contusions characteristically affect the orbitofrontal surface and anterior/inferior temporal lobes; diffuse axonal injury affects corpus callosum, grey–white junctions and brainstem.
diseases.progression: Some symptoms improve over weeks to months; moderate–severe injury may cause lasting impairment.
diagnosis: MRI for diffuse axonal injury and subtle lesions
diseases.imaging: CT shows haemorrhage, contusions and swelling; MRI is more sensitive for axonal injury.
treatments: Emergency stabilisation and prevention of secondary injury
Neurosurgery for haematomas or raised pressure
diseases.rehabilitation: Multidisciplinary rehabilitation: physical, cognitive, speech, vocational and psychological.
diseases.prognosis: Wide range from full recovery to severe disability.
diseases.prevention: Seat belts, helmets, fall prevention, safe sport practices.
diseases.emergingResearch: Blood biomarkers (e.g. GFAP) to guide imaging decisions.

faq.q: Why are the frontal and temporal poles commonly injured?
faq.a: They sit against rough bony surfaces of the skull base; acceleration–deceleration pushes the brain against them.

associations.explanation: Orbitofrontal contusions are typical.
Anterior and inferior temporal contusions are typical.
Diffuse axonal injury frequently involves the corpus callosum.
Severe diffuse axonal injury may involve the dorsolateral brainstem.

diseases.name: Concussion
diseases.overview: A concussion is a mild traumatic brain injury that temporarily disturbs brain function after a blow or jolt to the head or body.
diseases.pathophysiology: Rapid acceleration and deceleration cause a transient neurometabolic disturbance (ionic shifts, altered blood flow and energy mismatch) usually without visible structural damage on standard imaging.
diseases.causes: Sports, falls, collisions, assaults.
diseases.regionsSummary: A diffuse functional disturbance; no single structure is characteristically damaged on routine imaging.
diseases.progression: Most people recover within days to weeks; some have persisting symptoms.
diagnosis: Imaging only if red flags suggest more serious injury
diseases.imaging: Standard CT and MRI are typically normal.
treatments: Brief relative rest followed by gradual return to activity
diseases.rehabilitation: Vestibular therapy, graded aerobic exercise and cognitive strategies for persisting symptoms.
diseases.prognosis: Generally good.
diseases.prevention: Rule enforcement and technique in sport, helmets where appropriate, fall prevention.
diseases.emergingResearch: Biomarkers and advanced imaging to predict recovery.

faq.q: Why is no region highlighted?
faq.a: Concussion is a diffuse functional disturbance; highlighting one region would misrepresent it.

associations.explanation: Diffuse transient functional disturbance; not a focal structural lesion.

diseases.reviewStatus: Draft — educational summary from cited sources; pending clinical reviewer sign-off.

diseases.name: Diffuse axonal injury
diseases.overview: Diffuse axonal injury is widespread damage to axons caused by rotational acceleration–deceleration forces, a major cause of coma and disability after severe TBI.
diseases.pathophysiology: Shearing forces stretch axons, disrupting transport and leading to axonal swelling and disconnection. Lesions concentrate where tissues of different density meet.
diseases.causes: High-velocity injuries such as road traffic collisions.
diseases.regionsSummary: Grey–white matter junctions, corpus callosum (especially splenium) and dorsolateral rostral brainstem — the classic grading sequence.
symptoms: Cognitive, behavioural and motor deficits after recovery
diseases.progression: Recovery can be slow and incomplete.
diseases.imaging: CT may underestimate injury; MRI shows small haemorrhagic or non-haemorrhagic lesions in typical locations.
diseases.rehabilitation: Long-term multidisciplinary rehabilitation.
diseases.prognosis: Depends on severity and extent; brainstem involvement is associated with worse outcome.
diseases.prevention: Road safety measures, helmets.
diseases.emergingResearch: Diffusion tensor imaging biomarkers.

faq.q: Why can't the model show individual damaged axons?
faq.a: Axons are microscopic; the model shows where lesions typically cluster.

associations.explanation: Lesions at grey–white matter junctions (grade 1).
Callosal lesions (grade 2).
Dorsolateral rostral brainstem lesions (grade 3).

diseases.name: Hydrocephalus
diseases.overview: Hydrocephalus is an abnormal build-up of cerebrospinal fluid in the ventricles, which can raise pressure and damage brain tissue.
diseases.pathophysiology: Imbalance between CSF production and absorption, or obstruction of CSF flow. Non-communicating (obstructive) hydrocephalus is caused by blockage within the ventricular system (e.g. aqueduct); communicating hydrocephalus results from impaired absorption.
diseases.causes: Congenital (aqueductal stenosis, neural tube defects), haemorrhage, meningitis, tumours, head injury; normal pressure hydrocephalus in older adults.
diseases.regionsSummary: Ventricular system (lateral, third and fourth ventricles, cerebral aqueduct) with compression of surrounding white matter.
symptoms: Infants: enlarging head, bulging fontanelle, vomiting
Children/adults: headache, vomiting, blurred vision, drowsiness
Normal pressure hydrocephalus: gait disturbance, urinary incontinence, cognitive decline
diseases.progression: Acute hydrocephalus can be life-threatening; chronic forms progress gradually.
diagnosis: Lumbar drain trial or tap test for normal pressure hydrocephalus
diseases.imaging: Enlarged ventricles; the pattern helps locate an obstruction.
treatments: Endoscopic third ventriculostomy for selected obstructive cases
diseases.rehabilitation: Physical and cognitive therapy; developmental support in children.
diseases.prognosis: Varies with cause and promptness of treatment.
diseases.prevention: Prevention of preterm birth complications and CNS infections reduces some cases.
diseases.emergingResearch: Smart shunt valves and better selection for surgery.

faq.q: Is the whole ventricle diseased?
faq.a: The ventricles are enlarged by excess fluid; the highlight shows the system involved, not tissue disease.

associations.explanation: Lateral ventricles enlarge.
Third ventricle enlarges in many forms.
Aqueductal stenosis causes obstructive hydrocephalus.
Enlarged in communicating hydrocephalus or outlet obstruction.
Periventricular white matter is compressed and may show fluid signal.

diseases.name: Migraine
diseases.classification: Primary headache disorder (neurological disease of brain networks)
diseases.overview: Migraine is a common neurological disease causing recurrent attacks of moderate to severe headache, often with nausea and sensitivity to light and sound; some people have aura.
diseases.pathophysiology: Involves activation of the trigeminovascular system and release of neuropeptides such as CGRP, with altered processing in brainstem, hypothalamic and thalamocortical networks. Aura is linked to cortical spreading depolarisation, often in occipital cortex. There is no structural damage.
diseases.causes: Genetic predisposition with triggers such as hormonal changes, sleep disruption, stress or skipped meals.
diseases.regionsSummary: Network disorder: brainstem and hypothalamic modulatory centres, thalamus, and cortex (occipital cortex for visual aura). No region is structurally damaged.
symptoms: Visual or sensory aura in some people
diseases.progression: Episodic; may become chronic in some people.
diagnosis: Imaging only if atypical features or red flags
diseases.imaging: Usually normal.
treatments: Preventive: lifestyle measures, beta-blockers, certain anti-seizure medications, antidepressants, CGRP-pathway monoclonal antibodies, botulinum toxin for chronic migraine
diseases.rehabilitation: Headache diaries, trigger management, behavioural therapies.
diseases.prognosis: Often improves with treatment and with age in some people.
diseases.prevention: Regular sleep, meals and exercise; preventive medication when indicated.
diseases.emergingResearch: Further targets beyond CGRP (e.g. PACAP).

faq.q: Does migraine damage the brain?
faq.a: Migraine is a network disorder and generally does not damage brain structures; seek medical advice for new or changed headaches.

associations.explanation: Cortical spreading depolarisation in occipital cortex is linked to visual aura (functional, not structural).
Brainstem nuclei modulate trigeminovascular pain signalling.
Hypothalamic activation is implicated in the premonitory phase.
Relays and modulates head pain signals to cortex.

diseases.name: Chiari malformation
diseases.classification: Structural malformation of the posterior fossa / craniocervical junction
diseases.overview: A Chiari malformation is a structural condition in which part of the cerebellum (the tonsils) extends below the foramen magnum into the spinal canal.
diseases.pathophysiology: Often attributed to a small or crowded posterior fossa. Herniated cerebellar tissue can obstruct CSF flow at the foramen magnum and compress the brainstem and upper spinal cord; syringomyelia may develop.
diseases.causes: Usually congenital; occasionally acquired (e.g. CSF leaks).
riskFactors: Associated conditions: myelomeningocele (type II), connective tissue disorders
diseases.regionsSummary: Cerebellum (tonsils), medulla oblongata, fourth ventricle outflow and upper cervical spinal cord.
symptoms: Headache at the back of the head worsened by coughing or straining
diseases.progression: Many remain stable; some progress, especially with syrinx.
diagnosis: MRI of brain and cervical spine
diseases.imaging: Cerebellar tonsils extend below the foramen magnum; CSF flow studies may show obstruction.
treatments: Posterior fossa decompression surgery for symptomatic cases
diseases.rehabilitation: Physiotherapy as needed.
diseases.prognosis: Often good after surgery for appropriately selected patients.
diseases.prevention: Not preventable.
diseases.emergingResearch: Refining surgical selection criteria.

faq.q: Is Chiari malformation a disease?
faq.a: It is a structural abnormality rather than a disease process; symptoms arise from crowding and CSF flow obstruction.

associations.explanation: Cerebellar tonsils herniate below the foramen magnum (tonsils not separately segmented).
The medulla may be compressed.
CSF outflow at the foramen magnum can be obstructed.

diseases.name: Cerebral palsy
diseases.classification: Group of permanent developmental disorders of movement and posture
diseases.overview: Cerebral palsy is a group of disorders affecting movement, muscle tone and posture caused by non-progressive injury or abnormal development of the developing brain.
diseases.pathophysiology: Brain injury before, during or shortly after birth affects motor pathways. Patterns include periventricular white matter injury (common in preterm infants), deep grey matter injury, cortical-subcortical injury and malformations. The brain lesion does not progress, though its effects change with growth.
diseases.causes: Preterm birth, low birth weight, infections during pregnancy, perinatal stroke, hypoxic-ischaemic injury, genetic factors and malformations.
diseases.regionsSummary: Periventricular white matter and internal capsule (spastic diplegia), basal ganglia and thalamus (dyskinetic CP), cerebellum (ataxic CP), or unilateral cortical/subcortical injury (hemiplegia).
symptoms: Associated epilepsy, learning, vision or hearing difficulties in some
diseases.progression: Non-progressive brain injury; musculoskeletal effects can change over time.
diagnosis: MRI to identify brain injury pattern
diseases.imaging: MRI often shows periventricular leukomalacia, deep grey matter injury, infarction or malformation.
treatments: Selective dorsal rhizotomy in selected cases
diseases.rehabilitation: Lifelong multidisciplinary support.
diseases.prognosis: Highly variable; many people live full adult lives with support.
diseases.prevention: Antenatal magnesium sulphate for preterm birth and therapeutic hypothermia for neonatal HIE reduce risk in eligible cases.
diseases.emergingResearch: Early intervention and neuroprotection strategies.

faq.q: Does cerebral palsy get worse?
faq.a: The brain injury does not progress, although muscles and joints can be affected over time.

associations.explanation: Periventricular white matter injury is typical in preterm-born children with spastic CP.
Corticospinal fibres near the ventricles and in the internal capsule are injured.
Deep grey matter injury causes dyskinetic CP.
Thalamic injury accompanies basal ganglia injury in some.
Associated with ataxic CP.

diseases.name: Hypoxic-ischemic brain injury
diseases.classification: Acquired brain injury from oxygen or blood-flow deprivation
diseases.overview: Hypoxic-ischaemic brain injury results from inadequate oxygen delivery or blood flow to the whole brain, for example after cardiac arrest or around birth.
diseases.pathophysiology: Energy failure leads to excitotoxicity and cell death. Selectively vulnerable regions include hippocampal neurons, cerebral cortex, basal ganglia, thalamus and cerebellar Purkinje cells; watershed zones between arterial territories are at risk in hypotension.
diseases.causes: Cardiac arrest, drowning, suffocation, severe hypotension, perinatal asphyxia.
diseases.regionsSummary: Hippocampus, cortex, basal ganglia, thalamus and cerebellum; pattern depends on severity and duration, and differs between neonates and adults.
diseases.progression: Injury evolves over hours to days; recovery varies.
diagnosis: Neurophysiological and biomarker tests for prognosis
diseases.imaging: Diffusion restriction in cortex, basal ganglia, thalami or hippocampi depending on pattern.
treatments: Therapeutic hypothermia for eligible neonates with HIE
diseases.rehabilitation: Cognitive and physical rehabilitation.
diseases.prognosis: Depends strongly on duration and severity; prognosis should be assessed by specialists using multiple modalities.
diseases.prevention: Rapid CPR and defibrillation; good obstetric care.
diseases.emergingResearch: Neuroprotective adjuncts to hypothermia.

faq.q: Why is the hippocampus so vulnerable?
faq.a: Certain hippocampal neurons (CA1) are especially sensitive to energy failure and excitotoxicity.

associations.explanation: CA1 hippocampal neurons are among the most vulnerable to hypoxia-ischaemia.
Deep grey matter is vulnerable, especially in severe or acute insults.
Thalamic injury is common in severe injury.
Cortical laminar necrosis and watershed injury occur.
Purkinje cells are vulnerable.

diseases.name: Cerebellar ataxia
diseases.overview: Cerebellar ataxia is a syndrome of impaired coordination, balance and speech caused by dysfunction of the cerebellum or its connections. It has many causes.
diseases.pathophysiology: Damage to cerebellar cortex, deep nuclei or their pathways disrupts timing and calibration of movement. Midline (vermis) involvement mainly affects gait and trunk; hemispheric involvement affects ipsilateral limbs.
diseases.causes: Stroke, tumours, multiple sclerosis, alcohol, medications, vitamin deficiencies, autoimmune and paraneoplastic disorders, and inherited ataxias (e.g. spinocerebellar ataxias, Friedreich ataxia).
diseases.regionsSummary: Cerebellum and its connections through the pons and medulla (cerebellar peduncles) and the thalamus.
symptoms: Clumsy limb movements and intention tremor
diseases.progression: Depends on cause: acute (stroke), subacute (autoimmune) or slowly progressive (degenerative).
diagnosis: Genetic testing when inherited ataxia is suspected
diseases.imaging: May show cerebellar atrophy or a focal lesion, or be normal early.
treatments: Treatment of the underlying cause where possible
Omaveloxolone for Friedreich ataxia (approved in some countries)
diseases.rehabilitation: Physiotherapy (balance and coordination training), speech therapy, mobility aids.
diseases.prognosis: Depends on cause.
diseases.prevention: Limiting alcohol; addressing nutritional deficiencies.
diseases.emergingResearch: Gene-targeted therapies for inherited ataxias.

faq.q: Why does a cerebellar lesion affect the same side of the body?
faq.a: Cerebellar pathways cross twice, so each cerebellar hemisphere coordinates the same side of the body.

associations.explanation: Cerebellar dysfunction causes ataxia; pattern (midline vs hemispheric) shapes symptoms. Vermis and hemispheres are not separately segmented here.
Pontocerebellar connections.
Spinal and vestibular inputs via the inferior cerebellar peduncle.
Cerebellar output to motor cortex via thalamus.
